Data: 14 de setembro de 2026 (segunda-feira)

Local: Vila balneária de Alter do Chão, Santarém (PA)

Participação: Aberta ao público e voluntários

articles.title: Acidente com ônibus de excursão deixa 25 mortos em Cabo Verde | G1
articles.standfirst: O veículo transportava 32 pessoas que voltavam de um passeio próximo ao vulcão Pico do Fogo quando um pneu estourou; ônibus caiu em uma ribanceira de 30 metros.
articles.summary: O veículo transportava 32 pessoas que voltavam de um passeio próximo ao vulcão Pico do Fogo quando um pneu estourou; ônibus caiu em uma ribanceira de 30 metros.
articles.body:
Pelo menos 25 pessoas, a maioria crianças e adolescentes, morreram na noite de sábado (5) em um acidente de trânsito em Cabo Verde , durante uma excursão estudantil na ilha do Fogo.

As informações foram divulgadas pelas autoridades em um comunicado publicado neste domingo (6) pela rádio pública do país.

O ônibus transportava 32 pessoas que retornavam a São Filipe após um passeio nas proximidades do vulcão Pico do Fogo. A viagem fazia parte de uma atividade anual organizada para crianças pouco antes da volta às aulas, segundo autoridades locais.

Acidentes de grandes proporções são raros em Cabo Verde . O arquipélago da África Ocidental tem cerca de 550 mil habitantes e fica no Oceano Atlântico, em frente à costa do Senegal. Em geral, as estradas do país estão em boas condições.

Outras pessoas ficaram feridas, algumas em estado grave, informou José Canuto, responsável pela Defesa Civil do município de São Filipe.

Segundo testemunhas, um dos pneus do ônibus estourou. O motorista perdeu o controle do veículo, que saiu da pista e caiu em uma ribanceira de cerca de 30 metros de profundidade, em uma área de difícil acesso.

Segundo a imprensa local, que citou autoridades de saúde da ilha, sete corpos foram sepultados imediatamente devido ao estado em que foram encontrados. As causas do acidente ainda não foram determinadas.

O presidente de Cabo Verde , José Maria Pereira Neves, classificou o acidente como “uma grande catástrofe” em um comunicado publicado em sua página no Facebook.

De acordo com uma agência de notícias local, o presidente e outros integrantes do governo devem visitar a ilha neste domingo (6).

*Com informações das agências Agence France-Presse (AFP) e Associated Press (AP).

articles.title: Pedra sabão: por que a panela quebra e como isso se evita | G1
articles.standfirst: A panela de pedra sabão racha quase sempre por choque térmico. Entenda a causa e o passo a passo de cura e uso que faz a peça durar por gerações
articles.summary: A panela de pedra sabão racha quase sempre por choque térmico. Entenda a causa e o passo a passo de cura e uso que faz a peça durar por gerações
articles.body:
A panela de pedra sabão tem fama de durar gerações — e dura, quando bem tratada. Mas também é a que mais gera relato de rachadura. A causa quase sempre é a mesma: choque térmico . Entender por que a pedra racha e seguir alguns cuidados simples é o que separa a panela que passa de mãe para filha da que quebra no primeiro mês.

Panelas e travessas de pedra sabão: durabilidade que depende de cura e uso corretos — Foto: Divulgação / Panela de Ferro Fundido

A pedra sabão é rocha: aquece e esfria devagar, e não gosta de mudanças bruscas de temperatura . Colocar uma panela fria direto no fogo alto, ou jogar água fria numa panela quente, cria tensão interna que a rocha não absorve — e ela racha. Não é defeito da peça; é física do material. Todo o cuidado gira em torno de evitar esse contraste.

A pedra sabão racha por choque térmico: o contraste brusco de temperatura, não defeito da peça.

Antes do primeiro uso, faça a cura : esfregue óleo em toda a peça, por dentro e por fora.

Leve ao fogo bem baixo e aumente aos poucos, deixando a pedra absorver o óleo.

Repita a untada algumas vezes nas primeiras semanas de uso.

A cura sela os poros da rocha, reduz a absorção de líquido e aumenta a resistência.

Comece sempre no fogo baixo e aumente gradualmente.

Nunca coloque a panela quente sobre superfície fria ou molhada.

Não jogue água fria para lavar enquanto a peça está quente; espere esfriar.

Use difusor de chama em fogões potentes para distribuir o calor.

Com cura e uso corretos, a durabilidade é enorme. As panelas de pedra sabão incluem panelas, travessas e kits de panela mineira.

Sediada em Divinópolis , no Centro-Oeste de Minas, a Panela de Ferro Fundido trabalha com panelas de pedra sabão e ferro. As peças estão no catálogo de panelas de pedra sabão , com entrega para todo o Brasil.

articles.title: Justiça anula posse de servidora que assumiu cargo sem curso exigido | G1
articles.standfirst: Decisão da 2ª Vara Cível atende a uma ação proposta pelo Ministério Público Estadual (MPE). A servidora havia tomado posse em 2017.
articles.summary: Decisão da 2ª Vara Cível atende a uma ação proposta pelo Ministério Público Estadual (MPE). A servidora havia tomado posse em 2017.
articles.body:
Segundo o Ministério Público Estadual (MPE), a servidora tomou posse em 28 de dezembro de 2017 — Foto: Divulgação

A Justiça do Tocantins anulou a posse de uma servidora de Porto Nacional , na região central do estado, que havia assumido o cargo de Agente Municipal de Avaliação Imobiliária em 2017 sem possuir a formação técnica exigida pelo edital do concurso e pela legislação municipal. A decisão atende a uma Ação Civil Pública proposta pelo Ministério Público Estadual (MPE).

A sentença foi assinada pelo juiz Elias Rodrigues dos Santos, da 2ª Vara Cível de Porto Nacional, em 27 de agosto, e determina a desconstituição definitiva do vínculo da servidora com a administração municipal.

Segundo o Ministério Público Estadual (MPE), a servidora tomou posse em 28 de dezembro de 2017, mas não possuía, à época, o Curso Técnico em Transações Imobiliárias (TTI), requisito previsto na Lei Municipal nº 2.242/2015 e no edital do concurso público. A qualificação exigida só foi concluída em março de 2018, após o ingresso no serviço público. Por se tratar de uma sentença de primeira instância, ainda cabe recurso.

De acordo com a promotora de Justiça Thaís Cairo, responsável pela ação, a própria Prefeitura de Porto Nacional reconheceu a irregularidade ao instaurar uma sindicância administrativa que concluiu pela nulidade da posse. Apesar disso, o vínculo funcional não havia sido encerrado formalmente.

O g1 tenta localizar a defesa da servidora. A Prefeitura de Porto Nacional também foi procurada para se manifestar sobre a decisão, contudo, até a última atualização desta reportagem, não havia se pronunciado.

Durante o processo, a defesa sustentou que a servidora já possuía graduação em Engenharia Civil e curso de Perícias e Avaliação de Imóveis antes da posse. Com base nisso, argumentou que ela tinha qualificação equivalente ou superior à exigida para o cargo. O argumento, porém, não foi acolhido pela Justiça.

Na decisão, o magistrado destacou que não ficou demonstrado que a formação em engenharia civil pudesse substituir o curso técnico específico exigido para a função. Segundo ele, flexibilizar as regras previstas no edital para um candidato em particular violaria os princípios da legalidade, da isonomia e da vinculação ao instrumento convocatório.

A juíza também ressaltou que a legislação, bem como o entendimento consolidado dos tribunais, exige que todos os requisitos do cargo sejam comprovados no momento da posse. Dessa forma, a obtenção da qualificação profissional em data posterior não é suficiente para regularizar a situação.

A servidora já estava afastada cautelarmente do cargo por decisão judicial anterior, medida que havia sido mantida pela 2ª Câmara Cível do Tribunal de Justiça do Tocantins (TJTO) durante a tramitação do processo.

Na sentença definitiva, a juíza confirmou o afastamento e determinou que a Prefeitura de Porto Nacional adote as providências administrativas necessárias para cumprir a decisão.

O magistrado destacou que todos os requisitos previstos para o cargo devem estar integralmente preenchidos no momento da posse. O entendimento firmado é de que a obtenção da qualificação exigida após a nomeação não regulariza a situação.

Com isso, foi determinada a anulação da posse e o rompimento definitivo do vínculo da servidora com a administração municipal.

articles.title: 7 de Setembro em Porto Velho: desfile muda para a noite por calor | G1
articles.standfirst: Concentração será às 16h, na Avenida Santos Dumont, e desfile começa às 18h. Previsão indica máxima de 32 °C.
articles.summary: O desfile de 7 de Setembro em Porto Velho começa às 18h na Avenida Santos Dumont, com concentração às 16h, para evitar as altas temperaturas do dia.
articles.body:
Devido às altas temperaturas, o Desfile Cívico e Militar de 7 de Setembro será realizado à noite em Porto Velho neste ano. A concentração está marcada para as 16h, na Avenida Santos Dumont, próximo ao Espaço Alternativo. O desfile começa às 18h.

Para 2026, o governo de Rondônia decidiu transferir a programação para o período noturno por causa das altas temperaturas registradas durante o chamado verão amazônico.

Segundo a organização, a mudança foi feita para proporcionar mais conforto aos estudantes, familiares e ao público, reduzindo a exposição ao calor durante o evento.

A organização informou ainda que, à noite, as temperaturas são mais amenas e o local conta com iluminação adequada para a realização do desfile.

De acordo com o Instituto Nacional de Meteorologia (Inmet), Porto Velho terá muitas nuvens e pancadas de chuva isoladas na segunda-feira (7), feriado de 7 de Setembro. A temperatura deve variar entre 24 °C e 32 °C, com umidade relativa do ar entre 40% e 90%.

Segundo o Inmet, as temperaturas devem permanecer estáveis ao longo do dia. O instituto mantém ainda um aviso amarelo de perigo potencial para declínio da temperatura no sudoeste e sul de Rondônia.

O Desfile Cívico e Militar de 7 de Setembro de 2026 terá a participação das Forças Armadas, forças de segurança, órgãos de emergência, estudantes e entidades civis.

O desfile estudantil reunirá 13 escolas, incluindo unidades militares e da rede estadual. Algumas instituições também participarão com bandas de música.

Este será o segundo ano consecutivo em que Porto Velho realiza o desfile na Avenida Santos Dumont. Em 2025, o evento ocorreu pela manhã.

articles.title: Here's the industry that does not agree with the rest of America that is upset with AI data centers
articles.summary: Tech News News: As communities across the country push back against AI data centers over land use, water consumption and rising electricity costs, the trucking indust.
articles.body: As communities across the country push back against AI data centers over land use, water consumption and rising electricity costs, the trucking industry sees the buildout differently. With as many as two-thirds of AI data centers being constructed in rural areas, the influx of truck traffic is reshaping truck routes and is reportedly throwing a lifeline to a transportation business hit hard by macroeconomic uncertainty, from trade tariffs to increasing diesel prices.All the components that go into a data center, from HVAC systems to tubing and wiring and semiconductors, arrive primarily by truck, or by train and then truck. According to a report by CNBC, for a freight business hurt by successive rounds of trade war tariffs and surging diesel fuel prices, which hit an all-time high of $5.85 a gallon this week, AI data centers are providing a bit of a respite.Flatbed and heavy haul trucks see the biggest gains"Against that backdrop, AI and data center activity presents an opportunity for fleets," Patrick Brennan, senior vice president of fleet management solutions provider Cox Fleet, told CNBC. Overall freight demand is still uneven, he said, but AI is providing some needed stability. Equipment-led growth, whether for data centers or defence and semiconductor projects, is inherently more freight-generating, Fleet added.Some niches within the trucking sector are benefiting more than others, the report claims. The best-documented effect is the increased hauling of data center-aligned materials, which shows up in production indices and in individual carrier earnings commentary. Load-to-truck ratios have jumped as capacity tightening reaches this part of the market too."The effect shows up most in flatbed and heavy haul, where spot rates have hit multiyear highs this summer and capacity is tightest in construction-heavy markets," Brennan said. "Flatbed and heavy haul have been on an absolute tear since last year, and that's where demand from the buildout is most concentrated," he added.Because site location decisions for these projects are often determined by factors including power and land cost, the arrival of AI is also reshaping trucking lanes, with much of that freight moving into markets that were never traditional freight hubs. "This reshapes routes as much as it adds volume," Brennan said.The increase in large-scale construction projects is also creating additional demand for skilled transportation and fleet-related talent, and not just drivers."These projects require moving heavy equipment, generators, transformers, cooling systems, construction materials, and supporting infrastructure, which increases demand for CDL drivers, diesel technicians, fleet maintenance professionals, and logistics personnel," Brennan said.All of this is causing a scramble for personnel in what was an already shrinking pool, resulting in longer hiring timelines for specialised positions, increased recruiting activity, and higher demand for maintenance capacity as fleets operate more frequently or add equipment to support project-related freight. Also, more miles driven equates to more maintenance that needs to be performed.Smaller trucking companies getting a boost, but cash is tightIt's not just the big trucking companies that are seeing an AI boom, according to Jennifer Lockett, freight factoring operations manager at transportation financing firm altLINE. Smaller companies in the space are also seeing new business, but not without growing pains."Data center construction is creating new work for carriers, particularly those moving the massive transformers and generators needed to power these facilities, and large quantities of concrete and other construction materials," Lockett said.The size and specialised nature of these loads can also create opportunities for carriers to take on new customers and routes. And for smaller carriers, these projects can mean more consistent freight and opportunities to expand into new lanes."But they can also require additional trucks, drivers, and equipment to handle the increased volume. That can put pressure on cash flow, particularly when carriers take on larger customers or cover upfront costs for fuel, labour, and maintenance before getting paid," Lockett said.Carriers will need more working capital to manage that growth and additional expenses. "Still, the bigger story is how much new freight activity these projects can generate for trucking businesses," Lockett noted.Rural buildouts are rerouting freight trafficThe new trucking business related to data centers is rippling through the entire freight ecosystem. As construction ramps up in rural areas, it can increase demand for fuel, construction materials, and new drivers, which creates more trucking activity throughout the surrounding region.Janelle Griffith, global logistics practice leader at global risk management firm Marsh, said spikes in trucking traffic and routes are occurring now in Georgia and Texas."A lot of it is rural," Griffith said, pointing to research that shows 67 per cent of planned data center developments are in rural areas and 39 per cent of planned facilities are located in counties where there are currently none.Current freight demand vs. post-construction drop-offThe impact goes beyond the surge in flatbed leasing, Griffith said, with the data center itself only one component of a much larger AI-trucking effect that is impacting broad swaths of the economy."If we think about the supply chain, the data centers are not the end of the supply chain, but the center. They create rippling effects," Griffith said, adding that the effects spread to truckers, storage facilities, and warehouses. "Every phase of the data center itself creates opportunities," Griffith highlighted.Even when equipment and components can be brought in by rail, they still usually have to be trucked from the train terminal to the site. "A lot of things used to build data centers move via rail, truck takes it from destination to building, doesn't reduce demand, just reduced distance," said Kyle Roberts, vice chairman of industrial & logistics/capital markets at commercial real estate advisory firm Newmark Mountain West.He added that the short-haul aspect of a lot of the data center components has especially helped the LTL segment, which has been soft for some time, most notably seen in the 2024 bankruptcy of Yellow Trucking.But industry experts also warn of a potential overreaction to the AI trucking boom. Even with the new business, communities need to be careful about rushing to redo their entire infrastructure to accommodate freight since much of the AI data center-related business has an expiration date.Roberts said there is an "extraordinary drop off" in truck traffic to a data center once it is built. Compared to a typical 200,000-square foot warehouse or distribution center with 80 dock doors and two turns per day, a data center, once built, has a fraction of the truck traffic."Unlike warehouses that support large retailers or other physical goods delivery, data centers required comparatively little logistics support after they have been built," said Kyre Lahtinen, associate teaching professor of finance at Wake Forest University.Communities experiencing a boom in trucking should be cautious about how much infrastructure they build out, and whether demand will persist after the construction phase has passed, he said. For now, the AI ecosystem is active enough that truckers just move on to the next job."There is a massive ecosystem that sits around; all of those components have trucking demands. It's a very positive impact,” Roberts added.Get the latest technology news and updates. Download the TOI App.

articles.title: New Zealand home values hit three-year low as buyers remain cautious
articles.summary: News News: New Zealand’s home prices fell to their lowest level in more than three years in August, extending a downturn that began in the early 2022 and raising.
articles.body: New Zealand’s home prices fell to their lowest level in more than three years in August, extending a downturn that began in the early 2022 and raising concerns about the strength of domestic demand as the economy seeks to recover.The Home Value Index fell 0.4% after a revised 0.5% decline in July, property consultancy Cotality said in Wellington on Friday, September 4. Home values are now 18% below their January 2022 peak.The continued decline is adding to pressure on households already facing higher fuel costs and rising unemployment, suggesting that consumer spending is likely to remain subdued.The Reserve Bank of New Zealand (RBNZ), which raised interest rates for a second consecutive meeting this week, said the country’s economic recovery remained uneven. While exports and tourism are showing improvement, household consumption and business investment continue to lag as per Business Times.Cotality Chief Property Economist Kelvin Davidson said the housing market remained largely stagnant and was likely to stay that way into next year.“There’s no sign of a sharp downturn, but equally there’s no catalyst for stronger growth in the near term,” Davidson said.The RBNZ raised its official cash rate to 2.75 per cent on Wednesday as it moved to contain growing inflationary pressures.Policymakers indicated that another interest-rate increase is likely, while signalling they will take time to assess the economy’s response to the tightening measures already implemented.“Economic uncertainty, rising mortgage rates and a high level of properties available for sale are giving buyers little reason to rush,” Davidson said.The approaching general election in early November is also prompting investors to remain cautious, with uncertainty over the direction of future tax policy keeping many on the sidelines, he said.The centre-right coalition government is facing a difficult run-up to the Nov. 7 election, with the ruling National Party trailing in opinion polls. Voters are increasingly frustrated by the government’s claims of being a stronger economic manager as the recovery continues to struggle to gain momentum.New Zealand’s housing downturn is expected to last significantly longer than the decline that followed the Global Financial Crisis, when house values fell about 10% but recovered to pre-crisis levels within five years, Cotality said last month.The Reserve Bank of New Zealand said the prolonged weakness in the property market, sluggish income growth and job insecurity were continuing to weigh on household spending and domestic demand, according to the bloomberg report.The central bank expects house prices to decline 0.5% in 2026 before beginning a modest recovery, with prices projected to rise 2.4% in 2027 and 5.2% in 2028.Cotality Chief Property Economist Kelvin Davidson said a sustained recovery in house prices is unlikely until the labour market and job security improve significantly. He expects those conditions may not be met until well into 2027.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? Build Your Legacy with TOI Homes.

articles.title: 'We eradicated Naxalism, will eliminate narcotics': Amit Shah on drug-free India by 2029
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: Union home minister Amit Shah on Sunday said the Narendra Modi government has prepared a roadmap to make India drug-free by 2029, calling t.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Union home minister Amit Shah on Sunday said the Narendra Modi government has prepared a roadmap to make India drug-free by 2029, calling the fight against narcotics a national security priority.Addressing the media, Shah stated that the fight against narcotics has moved beyond isolated actions to become a coordinated national campaign.Shah said it was PM Modi’s objective that “drug-free youth power” would lead India towards Viksit Bharat by 2047. He said the government was committed to tackling narcotics with the same approach it used against Naxalism and terrorism.“Before 2014, the fight against narcotics was largely conducted in small units and isolation,” Shah said, adding that agencies had often focused on catching small-time accused. The government, he said, had now made the anti-narcotics fight a national security priority.Detailing the approach Shah stated that the government has strengthened its anti-narcotics drive through NCORD, state anti-narcotics task forces and joint coordination between agencies, along with the MANAS helpline and a revamped NCB. It also created the NIDAN database of narcotics offenders and a nationwide data-driven map of drug hotspots and trafficking patterns. The government now uses a “bottom-to-top” and “top-to-bottom” reverse investigation model, tracing small drug seizures back to their source and large consignments forward to their intended users to uncover the wider network.Shah also highlighted the government’s claims on internal security, saying terrorism in Jammu and Kashmir was declining and the sentiment of separatism had weakened since the abrogation of Article 370.He said those who had envisioned a Maoist “red corridor” from Tirupati to Pashupati had laid down arms and joined the mainstream, while more than 10,000 youths in the northeast had also surrendered their arms.Shah said Naxalism, which had persisted for five decades, had become a thing of the past. “We have eradicated Naxalism and will deal with menace of narcotics in the same manner,” he asserted.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: The annual Delhi Yamuna flood threat- why September matters?
articles.summary: India News: A year after the Yamuna inundated large parts of Delhi, the river is again flowing above the danger mark. The immediate threat may be lower this time,.
articles.body: A year after the Yamuna inundated large parts of Delhi, the river is again flowing above the danger mark. The immediate threat may be lower this time, but heavy rain in the upper catchment could quickly change the picture, exposing how vulnerable the city’s floodplain still remains.That vulnerability is built into Delhi’s geography. Every monsoon, as September sets in, the city watches the Yamuna closely because even a sharp rise in the river or a sudden surge in upstream discharge can quickly put thousands living and working along the floodplains at risk.The danger mark at the Old Iron Railway Bridge is 205.33 metres, while evacuation of vulnerable residents begins when the river reaches around 206 metres. On September 6, the Yamuna was flowing at 205.59 metres, already slightly above the danger mark.And it is not just the people living along the river who feel the impact. When the Yamuna rises sharply, critical roads and infrastructure can also be affected. The Loha Pul, a vital link between Central Delhi (including Kashmere Gate and Old Delhi Railway Station) and East Delhi, is among the key crossings vulnerable to rising waters during severe floods.2025: When the Yamuna broke its banksLast year, the warning turned into a full-blown crisis.The Yamuna crossed the danger mark and rose above 207 metres, inundating several low-lying parts of the Capital and forcing more than 10,000 people to evacuate vulnerable areas.The impact extended well beyond flooded homes. Roads and public infrastructure were affected, electricity supplies were disrupted and houses were left covered in mud and silt after the water receded. Thousands whose livelihoods depended on the floodplain also took a hit.Floodwaters reached the Ring Road and Outer Ring Road, disrupting traffic between Majnu ka Tilla and the Salimgarh bypass. The Municipal Corporation of Delhi stopped cremations at Nigambodh Ghat and the Geeta Colony ground because of flooding. Water-treatment infrastructure was also affected.A major factor was the enormous volume of water released from the Hathnikund Barrage in Haryana after intense rainfall in the upper Yamuna catchment.2026: Is Delhi facing another repeat?A year later, attention is once again turning to the Yamuna.The monsoon remains active, with heavy rain reported in parts of Delhi and northern India. The immediate concern is not simply the river’s current level, but how much water is being released upstream and whether intense rainfall in the catchment pushes those levels sharply higher.The Yamuna has remained comparatively stable this year, despite crossing the danger mark.Dr Shiv Singh Rawat, water expert and convener of the WalkForYamuna Campaign, said the difference becomes clearer when the upstream discharge is examined. “This year’s situation needs to be understood in its proper hydrological context. The maximum discharge released from Hathnikund Barrage during this year was around 64,000 cusecs, which is significantly below an extreme flood situation. That helps explain why Delhi experienced a much less severe river-flood situation than in 2025.”But that relative stability offers no guarantee.The India Meteorological Department has warned of isolated heavy rainfall over Haryana, Chandigarh and Delhi from September 10-12.Fairly widespread rain, accompanied by thunderstorms and lightning, is also likely over Uttarakhand from September 6-12, while rainfall disturbances are expected over Himachal Pradesh.For Delhi, what happens upstream can matter as much as what happens within the Capital itself.A spell of intense rainfall in the upper catchment can send a surge downstream, leaving communities along the floodplain with limited time to respond.The flood threat does not end with the water levelThe relatively stable Yamuna this year may have given Delhi a temporary reprieve, but the underlying vulnerability remains.The floodplain is not simply vacant land beside the river.It acts as a natural buffer during floods, helps recharge groundwater and performs an important ecological function.“The 2-km-stretch on both sides of Yamuna acts as a buffer for floods, restores groundwater balance and acts as an organic filter. However, excess rain will create flooding in Delhi, and sanitation is not adequate to handle floods in the Capital,” says environmentalist Kavita Ashok.Rawat warns that the greater danger could emerge gradually through construction and development. “The concern is that areas outside the most restrictive floodplain zones could gradually become corridors for permanent construction, infrastructure and commercial riverfront activity,” he says. “That would undermine the very floodplain functions that protect the city.”The question, therefore, is not only whether the Yamuna will rise this September. It is whether Delhi is becoming more or less vulnerable when it does.Living with the YamunaFor families living along Delhi’s floodplain, the monsoon is not simply a season of heavy rain. It is a recurring threat of displacement.When the river rises, families may have to move their belongings, livestock and essentials to higher ground with little warning.The granddaughter of Ramu Sahni, who lives with his family near the Yamuna floodplain, told TOI that residents don’t receive any advance warning.“We receive no warning on time. We see the rise in the water level of Yamuna and ourselves decide to shift to the roads with all our belongings. The authorities then notice the crowd on the roads and help us with tents.”Sahni, who came to Delhi from Bihar in search of employment many years ago, says the relief arrangements have also changed. “Earlier, they used to provide us with some ration and water in tents but now the situation has changed,” he says. “I don’t live here for free, I pay rent.”For many residents, simply relocating permanently is not an easy option.Their lives are tied to the floodplain through work, transport, markets and social networks. When the water recedes, they return.“We return back here when the water recedes after 2 months. This is all we have. I run a rickshaw, we are mostly ragpickers. Where will we go?”That cycle of evacuation, waiting, returning and rebuilding has become part of life for many families.Animals: The overlooked victimsFor families with livestock, evacuation is even more complicated.Leaving home is one thing. Moving buffaloes, cattle, calves and other animals to safety is another. Stray animals are even more vulnerable, particularly when rising water cuts off their escape routes.Sahni says livestock is not simply property for floodplain families, it is their livelihood. “People usually take their buffaloes with them on the roads. How will they earn? Now they have installed fencing around a small Yamuna pond here. How will buffaloes go there? They need to be there for survival. If a flood comes right now, there is no way we can rescue them immediately as there is only a small route to travel.”When asked who rescues stray animals during floods, he had no clear answer.PETA India told TOI that animals stranded during floods can face exhaustion, dehydration, hunger, injury and drowning, making rapid rescue and access to food, clean water and veterinary care critical.“The biggest challenge when trying to reach animals in emergency situations is getting to them in the first place. Access may be cut off by rising water, for instance,” said Sachin Bangera of PETA India.During last year’s floods, PETA India’s Rapid Response Team arranged a boat to rescue dogs stranded in flooded areas and at risk of drowning.“Animals who are left chained are the most vulnerable because they cannot escape, or they become exhausted and drown,” Bangera said.Aditi Bakshi, Animal Welfare Advocate and Specialist - Government and Public Policy at Mercy For Animals, says the problem goes deeper than rescue.“Many people are forced into an impossible choice by a system that gives them no option. Rescue boats and relief camps do not take animals. When the administration tells a family to evacuate and will not let them bring their cow, their pigs, or their two goats, the family has to choose between their children’s safety and the animal’s life.”She argues that flood preparedness must explicitly include animals.According to Bakshi, Delhi lacks a comprehensive operational framework covering animal evacuation, including a nodal officer, mapped animal shelters, pre-monsoon fodder stocks, evacuation protocols for large animals and regular drills. “A plan that has never been drilled is not a plan; it is a document,” she says.Delhi’s real test: Preparing before the next floodFor Delhi’s floodplain residents, the Yamuna may rise for only a few days. The disruption can last months.That makes flood preparedness about far more than issuing warnings once the river begins to rise.“Relief must be immediate, but rehabilitation must be humane and sustainable. People should not have to repeatedly rebuild their lives every monsoon,” says Dr Heera Lal Patel, IAS.During a flood emergency, he says, authorities need to provide clear information, accessible evacuation routes, transport and safe shelters. Vulnerable families cannot be expected to organise an evacuation on their own.Rawat argues that Delhi needs scientifically determined, risk-based floodplain zoning.“The real measures of success are: how many people are taken out of high-risk locations, flood-storage capacity restored and new encroachment prevented.”For companion-animal guardians, PETA India recommends identifying safe locations where pets will be accepted, keeping an emergency kit ready, and ensuring animals are microchipped or wear collars with updated contact details.But the larger challenge is institutional.The Yamuna’s rise is predictable. The exact scale and timing of a flood may not be.For communities living beside the river, that distinction can mean the difference between having time to evacuate and scrambling for safety as the water arrives.And every September, Delhi faces the same question: when the Yamuna rises again, will the city be better prepared, or will thousands once again be forced to leave their lives behind?Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: California mosque shooting: FBI warned parents about teen suspect’s dark-web activity days before attack
articles.summary: US News: The FBI warned the parents of one of the teenage suspects about his concerning comments regarding school shootings on the dark web just days before a .
articles.body: The FBI warned the parents of one of the teenage suspects about his concerning comments regarding school shootings on the dark web just days before a shooting at a California mosque left three people dead, according to a lawsuit filed by his mother.According to the Associated Press, federal authorities contacted the mother of Caleb Vazquez on May 14, warning her that her 18-year-old son had been making troubling remarks about school shootings online.Vazquez's mother allegedly passed the warning to staff at the mental health treatment facility where he was staying and receiving care.The FBI warning came days before Vazquez and another teenager, 17-year-old Cain Clark, allegedly carried out the shooting at the Islamic Center of San Diego. Three people, including a security guard, were killed in the attack before the two suspected gunmen were found dead inside a vehicle from what police said appeared to be self-inflicted gunshot wounds.Police had rushed to the mosque after receiving reports of an active shooter. San Diego Police Chief Scott Wahl said officers arrived within four minutes and found three victims dead outside the Islamic Center. Authorities also received reports of gunfire nearby, including an incident in which a landscaper at the site was fired upon but not hit.Dozens of police vehicles surrounded the Islamic Center as officers launched an active-shooter response and searched the mosque and an adjacent school. Authorities briefly placed the area under lockdown and urged residents to remain indoors before declaring the threat neutralised.The suspected shooters were later found dead in a vehicle in the middle of a nearby street. Wahl said they appeared to have died from self-inflicted gunshot wounds and that no police officers had fired their weapons.The lawsuit filed by Vazquez's mother alleges that Park Mental Health Treatment of San Diego failed to intervene despite warnings about her son's behaviour. Vazquez was receiving treatment there for mental health problems, including depression and psychotic episodes, according to the court filing.The lawsuit says Vazquez had previously been hospitalised after telling a classmate that he wanted to carry out a school shooting. Authorities had also flagged his behaviour a year earlier and confiscated 26 guns belonging to his father under California's red-flag law.Authorities have said Vazquez met Clark online and that the two were radicalised there. Police have not disclosed further details about their relationship or said whose weapons were used in the shooting.The mental health facility has disputed the allegations, saying neither Park nor its employees were responsible for Vazquez's actions.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: German business worried over possible far-right AfD election victory
articles.summary: Executives and business experts expect major difficulties for the economy in a German state where the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) seems poised fo...
articles.body:
German business leaders express concerns over potential economic impact of far-right AfD victory in Saxony-Anhalt election.

Executives warn that AfD's immigration and energy policies could harm state's attractiveness for skilled workers and foreign investors.

Siemens Energy CEO criticizes AfD's energy plans, labeling them as detrimental to German industry and democracy.

Executives and business experts expect major difficulties for the economy in a German state where the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) seems poised for victory in a keenly watched election on Sunday.

The main concerns involve investment and skilled workers from abroad, economist Monika Schnitzer told the Kölner Stadt-Anzeiger newspaper. "Given the party's election programme, it can be expected that if the AfD takes over the government, the state will become significantly less attractive as a location for skilled workers and companies."

Michael Hüther, director of the German Economic Institute (IW) think tank, took a similar view. "Anyone competing for foreign skilled workers must not strengthen a party that openly calls for their expulsion," he told the Rheinische Post newspaper.

An immigration policy based on the AfD's programme would be disastrous for Saxony-Anhalt, where the party is expected to secure a strong victory in Sunday's election, he said. There are concerns the party could secure enough support to govern on its own in the state.

Hüther added that, without immigration, demographic trends could cause the state's working-age population to shrink by around a quarter by 2045, leaving more than one non-working person for every person of working age.

Christian Bruch, chief executive of Siemens Energy issued an urgent warning on AfD energy policies in remarks to dpa. Their programme calling for a return to coal and nuclear power was bad for German industry and in some respects attacked democracy, he said.

"I consider that absolutely critical," he said. "Our company and our jobs in Germany depend on our ability to export, to attract international skilled workers to Germany, and on foreign investors being able to rely on political stability," Bruch said.

He noted that German domestic intelligence classified the AfD in Saxony-Anhalt as a "confirmed" right-wing extremist organization.

Bruch expressed disappointment that German politicians had failed to find compromises that most of the population could identify with, describing the situation as "absolutely critical."

He warned that other countries were undergoing rapid change and that the AfD was sending out a "dramatically wrong message" with its vision of returning Germany to past successes. "Nostalgic politics keeps setting us further back," he said.

The AfD's energy policies were "not sensible" in a highly interconnected Europe, he said.

In recent months, leading business executives have repeatedly warned about the AfD's economic plans. "Populist parties claim to have simple answers," Deutsche Bank head Christian Sewing said in Frankfurt recently.

"In reality, they advocate policies that run counter to the foundations of our success: openness, diversity, a strong Europe, reliable institutions and international cooperation," he added.

With polls suggesting that an absolute majority for the AfD cannot be ruled out, Sewing said he personally hoped "that this does not happen." From conversations with investors, he knew that many were deeply concerned about such an election outcome.

Munich economics professor Schnitzer, like Hüther, pointed out that many workers in Saxony-Anhalt would soon retire.

"Without an influx of people from outside the state, there will soon be a shortage of skilled workers. And without enough skilled workers, urgently needed investment will fail to materialize," Schnitzer said.

articles.title: China, Nepal race to find thousands still missing 12 days after floods
articles.summary: More than 5,500 people are still missing in China and Nepal after catastrophic floods across the two countries.
articles.body:
Rescuers in Nepal and Tibet are searching for thousands of people missing after catastrophic floods that have killed at least 1,384 people and left more than 5,500 missing, with challenges including deep mud, poor weather, and the risk of further landslides.

Nepal has requested aid from the United Nations-backed Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage to cover some of the staggering costs of the flood, appealing for $50m to help more than 84,000 people, with the country's Foreign Minister pointing to the responsibility of leading greenhouse gas emitters to compensate vulnerable nations like Nepal.

The flood, likely caused by a glacial collapse, has prompted calls for the global community to cover the cost of disasters afflicting developing nations like Nepal, with experts noting the increased frequency and scale of glacier floods as global temperatures rise, and the need for the UN fund to accept the request for aid.

Rescuers in Nepal are racing to reach thousands of people missing in areas near the China border after catastrophic floods as search operations enter their 12th day.

The flooding that authorities say was likely caused by a glacial collapse last month has killed at least 1,384 people and left more than 5,500 missing, among them about 800 foreigners, across the two countries.

In Nepal, rescuers have retrieved 1,341 bodies and are searching for about 4,996 people, the national disaster agency said on Sunday. In Tibet, the death toll has risen to 43, with 519 people missing, Chinese state news agency Xinhua reported.

Four people have been found alive since Friday, three of them in tunnels at hydropower facilities, where the government initially said about 100 people could be alive. Nepal's Energy Minister Biraj Bhakta Shrestha said teams at flooded hydropower tunnels were facing multiple challenges.

"Search and rescue is going on at the tunnels despite geography, adverse weather and lack of connectivity," he told the AFP news agency.

On the Chinese side, rescuers face deep mud, poor weather and the risk of further landslides that have slowed work in the narrow gorge.

Nothing remains of a five-storey customs building at Gyirong, once China's main land port with Nepal, where workers are digging with shovels, excavators and ground-penetrating radar to recover lost people.

The only road into Gyirong reopened on Wednesday, allowing heavy equipment in.

Nepal has issued a request that an untested climate emergency mechanism provide aid.

It is asking the United Nations-backed Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage – founded in 2022 to assist developing countries "particularly vulnerable to the adverse effects of climate change" – to cover some of the staggering costs of the flood.

The United Nations has appealed for $50m to help more than 84,000 people, saying the destruction makes delivering aid an immense challenge.

On Wednesday, Nepal's Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal pointed to the role of leading greenhouse gas emitters that have a "historical responsibility to compensate vulnerable nations like Nepal".

He added that the government has officially filed a "formal climate compensation claim letter" to international partners.

While the exact cause of the glacial collapse remains under investigation, experts say that the frequency and scale of glacier floods have increased as global temperatures have risen.

A United Nations study found that such floods have become nearly five times more frequent since 1950.

Manjeet Dhakal, lead adviser to the UN Least Developed Countries Group on Climate Change, says the global community has a responsibility to cover the cost of disasters afflicting developing nations like Nepal, and that the fund should accept the request.

Countries hit by such disasters are being forced to divert money set aside for health, education and development, he told Al Jazeera. "There are many cases where vulnerable countries are bearing their own cost," Dhakal said.

The flood was "not caused because of what Nepal has done in the past or in current form", Dhakal said, noting, "That's where the global community has a bigger responsibility to come in."

The UN fund has limited resources, he said. Indeed, its website reflects that it has received only about $631m of $822m in funds pledged by contributing states since inception, and has yet to spend out of the amount.

But, Dhakal said, even a "symbolic amount" could serve as an "inspiring lesson for the fund to justify what it was established for".

Al Jazeera's Nicolas Haque, reporting from a Buddhist monastery turned shelter in Kathmandu, said refugees there are still only just beginning to reckon with the trauma of the catastrophe.

"There are people meditating, praying, and there are children. It looks like there is a semblance of normal life," Haque said. "But make no mistake, I was talking to some of the children here. They've lost everything. They've lost their families, their homes, their parents."

About 200 people were brought by helicopter to the holy site, known as the Yellow Monastery, where doctors and volunteers have attended to them.

Haque spoke to a volunteer who had put out drawings for children to express their feelings.

"All of them put their stickers on 'happy', he said. Now why is that? The reason, he said, is that the children's emotions remain suppressed so soon after the crisis," Haque noted.

"What this volunteer told me is that in the days, months, or years to come, the floods will open, just like the floods open in the Himalayas, and emotions will be poured out."
authors: Al Jazeera Staff, AFP and Reuters

articles.title: Judge orders Trump admin to give 48-hour notice before work on 250ft Arlington arch
articles.summary: US News: A federal judge has ordered the Trump administration to notify the court at least 48 hours before carrying out any work at the site of a proposed 250-.
articles.body: A federal judge has ordered the Trump administration to notify the court at least 48 hours before carrying out any work at the site of a proposed 250-foot triumphal arch near Arlington National Cemetery.US District Judge Tanya Chutkan issued the order on Friday, a day after the Interior Department said it planned to begin work at the site despite an ongoing legal challenge and the monument still lacking final approval from a federal planning body.The order allows the administration to carry out archaeological work required under the National Historic Preservation Act. The exception covers efforts to determine whether underground cultural or archaeological materials are present.The government told the court it plans to excavate four test pits at the site from September 21 or later to check for artifacts and other cultural material. It said the area would be restored by October 31.Chutkan also reaffirmed an earlier agreement requiring the government to give 14 days’ notice before beginning construction. Any construction or demolition intended to prepare for construction before the National Park Service grants final approval would breach the court’s orders, she said.The dispute centres on whether the Trump administration has the legal authority to build the proposed monument. A group of military veterans and an architectural historian opposing the project argued in court that construction requires congressional approval.The administration has maintained that Congress effectively authorised the project through a 1925 law concerning Arlington Memorial Bridge. Opponents dispute that interpretation.Interior Secretary Doug Burgum had announced on Thursday that work at the site would begin after what he described as a lengthy wait. The government subsequently told the court that the planned excavation was intended only to investigate the site and did not amount to construction or demolition in preparation for construction.Chutkan questioned the administration’s authority to proceed with the project during a hearing in April. The government then agreed to provide advance notice before construction as part of a consent order.The proposed arch, designed to resemble Paris’ Arc de Triomphe, would stand near Arlington National Cemetery and rise 250 feet. Supporters say it would serve as a monument to American veterans.Opponents argue that the structure would damage the historic view between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington House across the Potomac River.The project also requires a decision from the National Capital Planning Commission, which is considering whether to allow the structure to exceed Washington’s usual 130-foot height limit.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Lebanon can sign Abraham Accords once Hezbollah is disarmed, Sunni MP says
articles.summary: “I don't see any reason why we cannot sign peace with Israel,” Makhzoumi said, adding that it was possible for Lebanon to “achieve” membership in the Abraham...
articles.body:
Lebanese Sunni MP Fouad Makhzoumi believes Lebanon can achieve peace with Israel and join the Abraham Accords once Hezbollah is disarmed and the country establishes control over its borders.

Lebanon's central bank is set to conduct an audit of transactions dating from October 2019 to December 2023, as the country scored poorly on Transparency International's Corruption Perceptions Index and seeks to restore investor confidence through financial reforms and regulatory frameworks.

Makhzoumi aims to attract new investment to Lebanon, encouraging the wealthy diaspora to return and rebuild the country, as emigration has surged due to economic instability, political uncertainty, and the influence of Hezbollah.

"I don't see any reason why we cannot sign peace with Israel," Makhzoumi said, adding that it was possible for Lebanon to "achieve" membership in the Abraham Accords.

Lebanon can join the Abraham Accords once Hezbollah is disarmed and can no longer use the country as a "launching pad" for attacks against Israel, Lebanese Sunni MP Fouad Makhzoumi told Middle East 24 last week.

Makhzoumi, who has previously urged the Lebanese military to demonstrate its willingness to confront Hezbollah's arms trafficking by establishing a checkpoint in Beirut's Dahieh neighborhood, said diplomatic relations and trade with Israel would be possible once "our side, as Lebanese, disarms the militias."

As it stands, he said, Lebanon has a border that is outside the state's control, allowing arms to be smuggled into and out of the country.

The CEO and executive chairman of Future Pipe Industries, a major international conglomerate, and the founder and leader of Lebanon's National Dialogue Party, he framed Lebanon's economic recovery and future growth as depending on the state's ability to tackle corruption within the judicial system and dismantle Hezbollah 's "parallel state."

Lebanon's central bank to conduct audit of transactions

Lebanon scored 23 out of 100 on Transparency International's 2025 Corruption Perceptions Index, ranking 153 out of 182 countries.

Makhzoumi's comments also came the same week that Lebanon's central bank announced that France-based consulting firm Alvarez & Marsal would conduct an audit of transactions dating from October 1, 2019, through December 31, 2023.

For Makhzoumi, restoring investor confidence requires more than financial reforms. He argued that capital will not flow into Lebanon until there is a regulatory framework that is fairly applied to every investor, one military force representing the country and one law applied equally to all.

Achieving those conditions, he said, requires Lebanon to disarm Hezbollah, "make sure that there is no opportunity for somebody to take me to a war under ideological reasons," establish a strong banking system that complies with international regulations, and "have peace with Israel."

Such a shift could also open the door to greater investment from Lebanon's regional partners. Notably, the United Arab Emirates, a signatory to the Abraham Accords, has become a major investor in Lebanon. UAE Foreign Trade Minister Thani bin Ahmed Al Zeyoudi led a delegation of more than 80 prominent figures to Lebanon last month, where the two countries signed an intergovernmental memorandum of understanding aimed at strengthening bilateral relations.

Regional analysts who spoke with The Jerusalem Post suggested that increased UAE investment could help Beirut distance itself from Iran and Hezbollah.

Makhzoumi said he is already in discussions with individuals interested in investing in southern Lebanon, where Hezbollah has created economic and social dependency by filling gaps in employment, healthcare and education.

Makhzoumi attempts to bring Lebanon's wealthy diaspora home

New investment, he argued, could encourage members of Lebanon's wealthy diaspora to return.

"I myself operate in 50 countries, and wherever you go in the world, you find a Lebanese that has been successful, whether in a big corporation, or in a state, or in an advisory role," he said. "So I am confident that the Lebanese will be willing to come and to build their country, but give me a state, give me a place that I can afford to bring my children back, and to make sure that they can live happily under the law, and not to be threatened by Hezbollah or by any other militia."

The lack of economic and political stability has driven many young Lebanese to seek opportunities abroad, Makhzoumi said. Many leave the country after graduating because they cannot envision a future in a country where assassinations occur, the threat of war remains, and Hezbollah can threaten their security.

That emigration has accelerated amid Lebanon's prolonged economic crisis, which began in 2019. According to figures published by the American University of Beirut, emigration increased by 450% in 2021 and 2022, with around 79,134 Lebanese citizens leaving the country in 2021 alone. The trend left a giant gap in numerous industries, especially in the healthcare sector.

articles.title: US envoys hold ‘substantive’ talks with Zelenskyy in first visit to Kyiv
articles.summary: Meeting comes a day after US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff met Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow.
articles.body:
United States special envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff have held talks with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on ending Russia’s war against his country, marking their first visit to Kyiv since the full-scale Russian invasion in February 2022.

The meeting on Sunday came a day after the two met Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow.

“It is very important that the delegation has arrived to see us. We have been waiting a long time for Steve and Jared, Witkoff and Kushner,” Zelenskyy said, thanking US President Donald Trump for “allowing them to come” despite the war. “To us, it is very important to do everything so that this war ends,” he added.

“We’ve had a very meaningful discussion, substantive, important, and we are very encouraged and we look forward to continuing this as long as it takes,” Witkoff said after the talks.

On his part, Kushner said that Trump wanted “not just to figure out how we end the current war, but how do we create the right conditions and arrangements for a long-term, durable peace,” adding that the US team had “learned a lot from the trip.”

Al Jazeera’s Audrey MacAlpine, reporting from Kyiv, said little new information came out of the talks.

“The thing that stood out is really that we haven’t learned very much new from it, sort of kicking the can down the road,” she said.

“President Zelenskyy saying that when it comes to the most important issues, like the issues of territory, that it would have to take place at the leader’s level, that is something that he has said time and time again,” MacAlpine added.

“But the real takeaway here was this visit in itself by the US envoys here to Ukraine, and the promise that they may return.”

Earlier, Zelenskyy published a video of himself meeting Trump’s envoys in central Kyiv, saying, “Talks have begun.”

Ukraine’s top security officials and negotiators were also present.

British, French and German national security advisers joined the Ukrainian president, Kushner and Witkoff for the second round of talks in the Ukrainian capital.

“We are grateful that the Europeans are with us today… Here we are all on the same side,” Zelenskyy said.

The US envoys arrived in the Ukrainian capital by train from Poland, hoping to revive negotiations to end Europe’s worst conflict since World War II after a summer of heightened tensions. While Witkoff and Kushner have visited Moscow eight times, they have never held talks in Kyiv until now.

Zelenskyy took the US envoys to see Kyiv’s historic Saint Sophia’s Cathedral, which sits opposite the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) security building that was hit by a Russian drone on Friday.

Moscow’s four-and-a-half-year invasion of Ukraine has killed hundreds of thousands of people and displaced millions.

Previous rounds of US-mediated peace talks encouraged by Trump, who campaigned on a promise to quickly end the war, have yielded few results. He suggested on Friday that the US had a fresh proposal, though he did not elaborate.

Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov described Saturday’s meeting in Moscow, which ran more than three hours, as “highly useful”, while a White House official told the Reuters news agency that the next steps would be announced in the coming weeks.

Ushakov called the talks “extremely frank”, saying the US team “put forward a number of ideas on possible routes to a settlement”, though he gave no details.

In televised comments before those talks, Putin said Russia would ensure the safety of the envoys while in Kyiv. “We will do everything that depends on us to ensure the safety of the negotiation process and mediators such as yourselves,” Putin told Witkoff and Kushner.

Earlier on Saturday, Putin had thanked Trump for persisting in his efforts to end the war despite it being “not simple”.

Trump said again on Friday that his envoys were bringing a “proposal” to end the fighting. “We have an idea for peace,” he said, without elaborating.

US efforts have so far failed to bring about a breakthrough in the war, in part because of the US-Israeli war on Iran.

Meanwhile, Russia has occupied large swathes of eastern and southern Ukraine, and Putin has insisted Moscow is intent on seizing the rest of the east.

In previous talks, the two sides have remained far apart on a range of key issues, including the future of Ukraine’s eastern regions of Luhansk and Donetsk. Russia has demanded Ukraine’s withdrawal from an entrenched belt of towns that it still controls there, but Kyiv has refused, reckoning it can still hold out for years.

For Ukraine, hard security guarantees from its European allies and the US are crucial to deter Russia from invading again.

Both Russia and Ukraine have pledged not to strike each other’s capital for three days around the US team’s visit. Yet despite the ceasefire agreement for the two cities, fighting continued elsewhere.

The Russian Defence Ministry said on Sunday that its forces had struck a Ukrainian cargo vessel in the Black Sea, which it said was carrying military equipment supplied to the Ukrainian army by Western countries, Russian state news agency Tass reported.

The ministry said earlier it had shot down 400 drones in the past 24 hours, according to the Interfax news agency.

It added that strikes were carried out during the day on Ukrainian infrastructure facilities used by the country’s armed forces, as well as drone storage sites.

The Ukraine Air Force, meanwhile, said Russia had attacked overnight with 108 drones and missiles. It also said on Sunday that it had struck the Ryazan oil refinery, about 480km (298 miles) inside Russia, overnight, causing a fire.

articles.title: Far-right AfD wins vote in Germany’s Saxony-Anhalt state: Exit polls
articles.summary: Party hails ‘historic’ result, but it is not immediately clear whether it will be able to form a government.
articles.body:
The Alternative for Germany (AfD) party has won the election in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, according to exit polls, becoming the first far-right party to take power at state level since World War II.

The AfD won 44.5 percent of the vote, exit polls for the ARD broadcaster suggested on Sunday. That is more than twice the 18.5 percent for the incumbent centre-right Christian Democrats (CDU), led by Chancellor Friedrich Merz.

“We have achieved exactly what we wanted to achieve,” said AfD’s lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund. “We have made history in this state.”

AfD co-leader Alice Weidel also hailed a “historic” result, which has given the far-right party a ‌clear mandate to govern, though it was not immediately clear whether it would be able to form a government.

“The reality is the AfD has got the lion’s share of the votes in this election, according to the exit polls. But the question is: is it enough to get them control of the state? Right now, we cannot say for sure,” reported Al Jazeera’s Dominic Kane from Magdeburg in eastern Germany.

Exit polls suggest the party has narrowly missed securing an absolute majority in the state parliament in Magdeburg.

Siegmund said he wanted to extend a hand to all parties willing to bring about a fundamental political transformation in the state. However, the AfD will not bend to other parties’ will, he stressed.

The AfD has never participated in a ruling coalition in Germany’s 16 states nor its federal government, as all other mainstream parties refuse to work with it, a policy infamously known as the “firewall”.

Sunday’s result is another blow to the authority of Merz, whose popularity has declined as ‌his coalition government struggles to revive growth in Europe’s largest economy.

His centre-right CDU came a distant second. Depending on the eventual count, the CDU’s state leader, Sven Schulze, would hope to still be able to form a new multi-party coalition to block the AfD from power.

AfD has tapped into a sense of nostalgia for communist East Germany, as well as lingering resentment about the enduring wealth gap with the west decades after the fall of the Berlin Wall in 1989.

In line with the sometimes defiant sense of local “Ossie pride”, Siegmund has often ridden the iconic local Simson bike, including to the polling booth on Sunday in his hometown of Tangermuende.

While Siegmund has been dubbed the friendly face of the AfD, his campaign promises have been radical, including targeting undocumented migrants with a “remigration and deportation offensive” from day one.

The party’s anti-“woke” agenda also includes promises to replace LGBTQ pride rainbow flags at public schools with the German standard and to change history teaching to lessen the emphasis on Hitler’s Third Reich.

In order to replace migrant workers, the AfD wants to lure back German expatriates, while offering “baby bonuses” for families to reverse the shrinking population in the small state of 2.1 million.

The German Economic Institute has warned that the AfD’s immigration policy would be “ruinous” for Saxony-Anhalt, which is highly reliant on foreign-born workers, especially in the health sector.

Others have voiced fears that an AfD-run state security apparatus could leak sensitive information to Russia, which Moscow could use to destabilise Germany.

The Kremlin “makes no secret of the fact that the AfD is the most important instrument for destabilising Germany for [Russian President Vladimir] Putin,” Thuringia state interior minister Georg Maier told the Handelsblatt daily newspaper.

images.caption: AfD candidate Ulrich Siegmund and party co-leader Alice Weidel celebrate after exit polls project victory in the Saxony-Anhalt state election, September 6, 2026. [Tobias Sschwarz/AFP]

articles.title: Germany’s far-right AfD projected to win eastern state but unclear if it will be able to govern
articles.summary: ‌The far-right Alternative for Germany surged into first place in state elections in Saxony-Anhalt on Sunday but it was unclear whether it would be able to form a government on its own, according to exit polls after voting closed.
articles.body: ‌The far-right Alternative for Germany surged into first place in state elections in Saxony-Anhalt on Sunday but it was unclear whether it would be able to form a government on its own, according to exit polls after voting closed. The AfD won 44.5% of the vote, with Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s conservatives on 18.5%, with the center-left Social Democrats and environmental Greens both clearing the minimum threshold to enter parliament, an exit poll on the ARD broadcaster showed. “We have made history in this country,” said Ulrich Siegmund, the 35-year-old AfD lead candidate in Saxony-Anhalt, who drew thousands to his campaign rallies and who repeatedly cast victory in the state as a first step toward securing national power in federal elections due in 2029. The result marks a major advance in the AfD’s push for national power and a significant setback for Merz’s coalition government, although it remained unclear whether the party would be able to form a state government. Turnout was around 76%, well above levels typically seen in state elections. Much could depend on whether the left-wing populist BSW party, a potential AfD coalition partner, could also clear the threshold. Exit polls showed it just above or just below it. State premier Sven Schulze congratulated the AfD and acknowledged the result showed it was the strongest party. If the AfD is unable to rule outright, it could trigger a protracted process of coalition building by mainstream parties who are determined to keep out of power a party investigated for right-wing extremism by Germany’s domestic intelligence service. The AfD’s program includes plans to push schools and cultural institutions toward more traditional values, curb immigration and overhaul public broadcasting. While hard right parties have gained ground elsewhere in Europe, Germany’s Nazi past has contributed to a reluctance among mainstream parties to cooperate with the AfD, which wants a hard line on migration and warmer ties with Russia. The AfD sees accusations of extremism as scaremongering and an insult to its millions of supporters. Siegmund told CNN the election result will give his party the mandate to return to “sensible diplomacy” with both Russia and the United States. “We need both if we as Germany want to be successful,” he said. Alice Weidel, the party’s co-leader who called it an “historic” result, also told CNN: “We stood for election very clearly to represent the interests of our country — not Ukraine’s, not any other country’s.” Sunday’s result is also another blow to the authority of Merz, whose popularity has sagged as his coalition government struggles to revive growth in Europe’s largest economy. Describing Merz’ premiership as a “catastrophe,” Weidel labeled the AfD “a people’s party” that will seek to “deport everyone obligated to leave the country” and close the borders if given the mandate to govern at the federal level. In a fracturing political landscape, the AfD is now Germany’s most popular party nationally, though other parties have ruled out forging coalitions with the AfD in a policy known as the “firewall.” This story has been updated. CNN reporting from Sebastian Shukla contributed to this story.

articles.title: Wright says Iran war worth it to ‘reset’ Middle East
articles.summary: Energy Secretary Chris Wright said Sunday the Iran war is necessary, arguing the U.S. needs to “reset” the Middle East. During an interview on ABC News’s “This Week,” Wright reiterated the longstanding talking point from administration officials that the goal of the conflict is to prevent Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon. “A nuclear-armed Iran…
articles.body:
Energy Secretary Chris Wright said Sunday the Iran war is necessary , arguing the U.S. needs to “reset” the Middle East.

During an interview on ABC News’s “This Week,” Wright reiterated the longstanding talking point from administration officials that the goal of the conflict is to prevent Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon.

“A nuclear-armed Iran is an existential threat, not just for the region, but for the world economy,” he told host Martha Raddatz.

“I’m very proud of President Trump, not just kicking this can down the road like previous presidents have done, but saying we’ve got to end that capability,” Wright added. “We’ve got to reset the Middle East so it can have generations of peace and prosperity.”

The war, in its seventh month, has resulted in the deaths of 18 American service members and thousands of Iranian civilians. The U.S. and Iran continued to exchange strikes this weekend, and there is no sign of a deal to permanently end hostilities.

The conflict has also come with economic costs for the U.S., stemming from the Iranian military’s restrictions on shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.

The national average price of a gallon of regular gas is roughly $4.14 on Sunday, more than six months after it was below $3 just days before the U.S. and Israel launched the war, according to AAA.

Labor Day weekend travelers, in fact, are seeing the highest prices at the pump on record, AAA reported on Thursday .

Wright said Sunday that daily transit in the Strait of Hormuz is at roughly “two-thirds” of where it stood before the war, as the U.S. military has sought to escort tankers through the waterway.

The Energy secretary noted his estimate of transit in the strait includes oil passing through pipelines .

“They’re clinging on to power as the United States continues to escalate the volume of oil that transits through the Strait of Hormuz,” Wright said, referring to the Islamic Republic regime.

articles.body:
Rep. Mike Lawler (R-N.Y.) on Sunday broke with President Trump regarding the commander in chief’s recent statement about the Iran war where he downplayed the conflict .

“Any time you are at war or in a military escalation, it is certainly not small potatoes. It is serious. I think we all recognize that,” Lawler told CNN’s Dana Bash on “State of the Union,” referencing recent comments from the president.

“Ensuring Iran does not possess a nuclear weapon, stopping them from continuing to finance terrorism, Hamas, Hezbollah, the Houthis, and other terror proxies, stopping them from mass-producing ballistic missiles, drones, which are being used by Russia against Ukraine, is critical,” he added.

In the Oval Office on Friday, Trump said he was referring to the Iran war as “a military conflict because it’s small potatoes for us.”

“It’s not a big thing,” the president added.

The Iran war just passed the six-month mark, with the fighting straining U.S. relationships with historic allies, driving up oil and gas prices and proving unpopular with the American public in recent polling.

On Sunday, Energy Secretary Chris Wright said he did not “want to have an opinion” on the direction of gas prices Americans are paying, which are above $4 per gallon on average.

“You said on this show five months ago that high gas prices had peaked, but between not just the Iran war, but the Russia-Ukraine war and the U.S.’s own dwindling reserves, isn’t it possible gas prices could go up even more?” Bash asked Wright on “State of the Union.”

“Look, I don’t want to have an opinion on that, but if you look at the futures market right now, what can you buy gasoline for two months in advance from where we are today? It’s down more than 30 cents a gallon from where it is today,” Wright responded.
